headline: Good conversations mix one topic with new ideas

sources.title: Want to have a better chat? Scientists say the secret is 'pink noise' (The Guardian)
Pink noise makes conversations more enjoyable (EurekAlert!, Science Advances press release)
How "Pink Noise" in Conversation Makes Chats Enjoyable (Neuroscience News)

chunks.text: Scientists at Dartmouth College, a university in the U.S. state of New Hampshire, have studied what makes a chat [[enjoyable]]. Their study was published on November 6, 2026. The researchers say it is hard to {{figure out}} why some talks feel great. They {{looked into}} this question using more than 1,000 conversations between [[strangers]]. After each chat, both people {{filled out}} a [[survey]].

verbs.wrong: To record a talk for later study
verbs.why: She never figures out the rules of that card game. Most kids figure out the new phone in a few minutes. The researchers say it is hard to figure out why some talks feel great.

verbs.wrong: To ask a stranger to join a chat
verbs.why: Scientists look into why some people sleep better than others. Good reporters look into a story before they write it. The scientists looked into this question using more than 1,000 conversations between strangers.

verbs.correct: To complete a form or survey
verbs.wrong: To read a form aloud to someone
verbs.why: New patients fill out a form at the front desk. Students fill out a short survey at the end of each class. After each chat, both people filled out a survey.

chunks.text: The most enjoyable conversations had a [[balance]] between staying on one [[subject]] and moving to new ideas. People stayed on a subject long enough to understand it and [[get to know]] each other. Then one person {{brought up}} something new, and the other {{picked up on}} it. A chat can fail in two ways. First, it can {{jump around}} all the time, or one person can [[ignore]] the other's replies. Second, people can [[repeat]] each other's words and {{end up}} bored.

verbs.wrong: To share the same view as someone
verbs.why: My aunt always brings up politics at dinner. He never brings up money with his friends. In good chats, one person brought up something new.

verbs.correct: To notice something and say more about it
verbs.why: Good listeners pick up on what you say and ask more. My best friend always picks up on my hints and asks about them. In good chats, the other person picked up on the new idea.

verbs.correct: To change quickly from one subject to another
verbs.wrong: To speak louder than the other person
verbs.why: His stories jump around, so they are hard to follow. Our meetings jump around when there is no plan. A chat can fail when it jumps around all the time.

verbs.correct: To finally reach a certain state
verbs.wrong: To try hard to look interested
verbs.why: People who skip breakfast often end up hungry by ten. If you stay up too late, you end up tired at work. People who just repeat each other's words can end up bored.

chunks.text: Scientists call this balanced pattern "pink noise," a physics term for patterns not too steady or too random. More pink noise meant people enjoyed a chat more and felt a stronger [[connection]]. The team also studied talks between friends to {{find out}} if this was true for them. It was. In [[speed dating]], single people have short talks with many [[possible partners]]. There, more pink noise [[predicted]] which pairs {{met up}} for a [[second date]].

verbs.correct: To learn a fact by checking
verbs.why: I call the store to find out when it opens. Doctors run tests to find out what is wrong. The team studied talks between friends to find out if this was true for them.

verbs.correct: To see someone at a set time and place
verbs.wrong: To talk on the phone for hours
verbs.why: My old classmates meet up once a year. We meet up for coffee every Friday. More pink noise predicted which speed-dating pairs met up for a second date.

chunks.text: The team also studied podcasts with two [[hosts]]. Their talks became more balanced over the first 50 [[episodes]]. The study's [[lead author]] thinks people can learn this skill. In her view, practice can {{pay off}}. When the team asked a chatbot to {{come up with}} enjoyable and boring conversations, the enjoyable ones had more pink noise. A conversation expert at a London university [[praised]] the study. But she {{pointed out}} that many of life's most important talks are [[painful]], not enjoyable.

verbs.why: Hard work usually pays off in the end. Her daily piano practice pays off at every concert. The lead author thinks that practice can pay off in conversation.

verbs.correct: To create a new thing or idea
verbs.why: My son comes up with a new game every weekend. Good writers come up with fresh ideas. The team asked an AI chatbot to come up with enjoyable conversations.

verbs.wrong: To change the subject of a talk
verbs.why: My doctor points out that sleep matters for health. Our teacher often points out common mistakes. The expert pointed out that many important talks are painful, not enjoyable.

ex: I can't figure out why my laptop is so slow.
It took me a week to figure out the bus system.
We finally figured out what the baby wanted.
The company promised to look into my complaint.
A reporter is looking into the rise in rent prices.
Can you look into why the bill is so high?

vocab.def: To complete a form or survey
ex: Please fill out this form before your appointment.
I filled out three job applications today.
You need to fill out a form to get a library card.
Don't bring up her old boyfriend at the party.
I brought up the idea of a vacation, and everyone liked it.
She brought up a good question at the meeting.

vocab.def: To notice something and say more about it
ex: She picked up on my comment about Paris and asked about my trip.
A good host picks up on each guest's story and asks a follow-up question.
He picked up on my idea and added his own thoughts.

vocab.def: To change quickly from one subject to another
ex: The movie jumps around in time, so pay attention.
Her emails jump around from one problem to the next.
Try not to jump around when you give a speech.

vocab.def: To finally reach a certain state
ex: We got lost and ended up late for the wedding.
If you don't save money, you may end up in debt.
He ended up happy with his choice of college.

vocab.def: To learn a fact by checking
ex: I want to find out who won the game.
She found out that her flight was canceled.
Let's find out how much the tickets cost.

vocab.def: To see someone at a set time and place
ex: Let's meet up after work for a drink.
The two families meet up every summer at the lake.
We met up at the mall and went shopping together.
All those early runs paid off when she won the race.
Studying every night really paid off on the final test.
Being kind to customers pays off for small shops.

vocab.def: To create a new thing or idea
ex: We need to come up with a name for the new dog.
She came up with a smart plan to save money.
Can you come up with a good title for the report?
He pointed out that the store closes early on Sundays.
My friend pointed out a typo in my resume.
The guide pointed out that the bridge is very old.

wordDefs.def: Giving you pleasure and making you feel good
ex: We had an enjoyable evening with our neighbors.
The hike was long but very enjoyable.
She finds cooking more enjoyable than cleaning.
Parents tell children not to get into cars with strangers.
Two strangers helped me push my car.
On the train, I sat between two strangers.

wordDefs.def: A set of questions that many people answer
ex: The hotel sent me a survey after my stay.
A survey showed that most workers want shorter meetings.
Only half of the students answered the survey.

wordDefs.def: A good mix where no part is too strong or too weak
ex: It is hard to find a balance between work and family.
This soup has a nice balance of salt and spice.
A healthy diet needs a balance of different foods.

wordDefs.def: The main topic of a talk or text
ex: Money is a hard subject for many couples.
Let's change the subject before we start to argue.
The subject of the meeting was the new budget.

wordDefs.def: To slowly learn what a person is like
ex: It takes time to get to know new coworkers.
I want to get to know my neighbors better.
Team dinners help players get to know each other.

wordDefs.def: To pay no attention to someone or something
ex: He tends to ignore emails from his bank.
Try to ignore the noise and focus on your test.
Please don't ignore me when I am talking to you.

wordDefs.def: To say the same words again
ex: Could you repeat the question, please?
The teacher asked us to repeat each new word.
My little brother likes to repeat everything I say.

wordDefs.def: A feeling of being close to another person
ex: She felt a strong connection with her new roommate.
Playing music together gives the band a real connection.
Many people want a deeper connection with their friends.

wordDefs.def: An event where single people meet many others in short talks
ex: My cousin met her husband at a speed dating night.
Speed dating events often give each pair five minutes.
He tried speed dating because he was too busy to date.

wordDefs.def: People who could become someone's boyfriend or girlfriend
ex: Dating apps show users many possible partners.
She met several possible partners at the event.
He likes to meet possible partners in person first.

wordDefs.def: Showed what was likely to happen
ex: The weather report predicted rain for the weekend.
Her test scores predicted how well she did in college.
Few experts predicted that the small team would win.

wordDefs.def: A second planned meeting between two people who like each other
ex: After a great first dinner, he asked her for a second date.
They went bowling on their second date.
She was nervous before their second date.

wordDefs.def: People who lead and talk on a show
ex: The two hosts of the morning show are old friends.
Radio hosts often take calls from listeners.
The game show has new hosts this season.

wordDefs.def: Single parts of a series, like a TV show or podcast
ex: I watched three episodes of the show last night.
The podcast puts out new episodes every Monday.
Each season has ten episodes.

wordDefs.def: The main writer of a science study
ex: The lead author spoke to reporters about the results.
She was the lead author on her first study at age 25.
The lead author thanked the whole team.

wordDefs.def: Said good things about someone or something
ex: The coach praised the players after the game.
Critics praised the movie for its music.
My boss praised my report in front of everyone.

wordDefs.def: Making you feel sad or hurt
ex: Saying goodbye to her old dog was painful.
The divorce was painful for the whole family.
It is painful to read about the accident.

mainIdea.s: Researchers found that people enjoy a talk most when they stay with one subject for a while and then add fresh ideas. Pairs with this balance also felt closer and were more likely to date again.
mainIdea.why: The best chats had a balance between one subject and new ideas. More of this pattern also predicted which speed-dating pairs met up for a second date.

mainIdea.s: A study of over a thousand chats shows that the best talks mix one subject with fresh ideas. But the researchers say this balance comes only from personality, so practice does not help at all.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the lead author thinks people can learn this skill. Podcast hosts became more balanced over their first 50 episodes.

mainIdea.s: Scientists in New Hampshire report that adults who talk with strangers on the bus each morning feel happier at work. They now want cities to add quiet seats and talking seats on every bus.
mainIdea.why: The study looked into what makes a conversation enjoyable. It found a balance between staying on one subject and bringing up new ideas.

tf.s: The researchers looked into conversations between strangers.
tf.why: They studied more than 1,000 chats between people who did not know each other.

tf.s: The most enjoyable chats stayed on one subject from start to finish.
tf.why: People stayed on one subject for a while, and then one person brought up something new.

tf.s: In good chats, the other person picked up on the new idea.
tf.why: One person brought up something new, and the other person noticed it and talked about it.

tf.s: People who only repeat each other's words end up enjoying the chat more.
tf.why: They can end up bored. Repeating each other's words is one way a chat can fail.

tf.s: More pink noise predicted which speed-dating pairs met up again.
tf.why: Pairs with more of this balanced pattern were more likely to meet up for a second date.

tf.s: The conversation expert said all important talks are enjoyable.
tf.why: She pointed out that many of life's most important talks are painful, not enjoyable.

lines.text: Did you see the new study about what makes a good conversation?
No. Can scientists really {{figure out}} something like that?
They tried. A team at Dartmouth {{looked into}} more than a thousand chats between strangers.
How did they know which chats went well?
After each talk, both people {{filled out}} a survey.
So what's the secret? Better [[small talk]]?
Balance. You stay on one subject for a while. Then someone {{brings up}} something new, and the other person {{picks up on}} it.
So you can't just {{jump around}} from one thing to the next.
Right. But you also shouldn't repeat each other [[word for word]], or you {{end up}} bored.
That sounds like my last date.
[[Funny you should say that]]. In speed dating, this balance predicted which pairs {{met up}} again.
So a good conversation is a skill?
The lead author thinks so. Hosts of two-person podcasts got more balanced in their first fifty episodes.
So practice can {{pay off}}. But [[it takes two]], right?
[[You said it]]. Both people have to listen.
Did any experts have doubts about the study?
One expert {{pointed out}} that some of the most important talks are painful, like a hard goodbye.
That's true. Not every good talk is a fun one.

expressions.def: Light, polite talk about easy subjects like the weather
ex: I'm not good at small talk at parties.
We made small talk while we waited for the doctor.

expressions.def: Used to say that someone uses exactly the same words
ex: She repeated the speech word for word.
Don't copy your friend's homework word for word.

expressions.def: Used when someone mentions a thing you just planned to mention
ex: Funny you should say that. I just bought the same shoes.

expressions.def: Used to say that both people share the work or the blame
ex: A good marriage needs effort, and it takes two.
Don't blame only him for the fight. It takes two.

expressions.def: Used to strongly agree with what someone just said
ex: You said it. That movie was much too long.
"This traffic is terrible." "You said it."
